extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying and overcoming obviousness rejections (35 U.S.C. 103) where prior art is copending or commonly owned, including statutory disqualification under 35 U.S.C. 103(c), CREATE Act effects, and evidentiary/ procedural requirements (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit, affidavits, terminal disclaimers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional obviousness rejection based on provisional 102(e) prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional rejections of the obviousness type under 35 U.S.C. 103 based on provisional prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) are applied to copending applications having different effective filing dates wherein each application has a common assignee or a common inventor; the earlier filed application, if patented or published, would constitute prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a rejection is provisional because the subject matter and the prior art are pending applications. It alerts the applicant and signals that action is needed to avoid an actual rejection if one application issues. If the copending applications are later combined into a single application and restriction/division issues arise, 35 U.S.C. 121 may preclude use of a patent issuing therefrom as a reference against the other application. Examples illustrate various fact patterns (e.g., employees A and B, common assignee C) showing when provisional 103 rejections and provisional double patenting rejections are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome provisional 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (A–E)
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisional 103 rejection based on a copending earlier-filed application can be overcome by specific actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (A) Argue patentability over the earlier-filed application. (B) Combine the subject matter of the copending applications into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and abandon the copending applications — note: claims in the later application relying on prior applications may not get 120 benefit unless each claim is supported by the earlier disclosure in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. (C) File an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation (that the unclaimed invention was derived from the inventor of the other application) so it is not "invention by another." (D) File an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing a date of invention prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the copending application. (E) For applications pending on/after Dec. 10, 2004, show that (1) the prior art and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person when the invention was made, or (2) the subject matter is disqualified under the CREATE Act amendment to 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (i.e., joint research agreement disqualification). Additionally, where the applications claim the same patentable invention, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 may be used to overcome a 103 rejection in a common ownership situation if the earlier application has been published or matured into a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) prior-art disqualification for common ownership or joint research agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art only under subsections (e), (f), or (g) of 35 U.S.C. 102 shall not preclude patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the claimed invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purposes of 103(c), subject matter and a claimed invention shall be deemed owned by the same person if: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. The term "joint research agreement" means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement between two or more persons/entities for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field. Important limits: 103(c) applies only to obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 and does not affect anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102 or double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date and scope rules for 103(c) and CREATE Act
rubrics_metrics.description: The CREATE Act (Dec. 10, 2004) amended 35 U.S.C. 103(c) to broaden disqualification to prior art under 102(e) as well as (f) and (g), effective for patents granted on or after Dec. 10, 2004; AIPA (Nov. 29, 1999) earlier added some exclusions effective for applications filed on/after that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2004 amendment (CREATE) applies to patents granted on or after Dec. 10, 2004 (including reissues granted on/after that date). For reexamination or reissue proceedings, whether 103(c) (as amended) applies depends on the grant date of the patent being examined. The CREATE Act does not affect final decisions rendered prior to Dec. 10, 2004. The change allowing exclusion of subject matter that is prior art only under 102(e) is also applicable to applications filed prior to Nov. 29, 1999 if pending on Dec. 10, 2004 (per CREATE Act effective-date provisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: 103(c) does not disqualify anticipatory 102 references or double patenting rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) applies only to prior art usable in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103; subject matter that qualifies as anticipatory prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 is not affected and may still be used to reject claims as anticipated. Double patenting rejections based on subject matter disqualified under 103(c) should still be made as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should continue to make 102 anticipation and double patenting rejections where appropriate. 103(c) cannot be relied on to overcome or prevent an anticipation rejection or a double patenting rejection. See 37 CFR 1.78(c) and MPEP § 804 for double patenting practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'commonly owned' for 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly owned means wholly owned (100%) by the same person(s) or organization(s) at the time the invention was made; if less than 100% ownership of either the reference or the claimed invention exists among the same owners, common ownership does not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an invention/application is owned by multiple entities and they seek exclusion under 103(c), the reference must have been owned by or subject to obligation of assignment to the same entities that owned the application at the time the later invention was made. Examples given: parent/subsidiary ownership percentages illustrating when common ownership exists or not. A license where the owner retains basic ownership rights does not defeat common ownership. The requirement is temporal: ownership must exist at the time the claimed invention was made; post-invention common ownership is insufficient. Moral or unenforceable obligations are not adequate evidence of common ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and evidence required to establish disqualification under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of establishing that subject matter is disqualified as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) rests upon the person urging disqualification (e.g., applicant or patentee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner, having established a prima facie case of obviousness based on the subject matter, will place the burden on applicant to provide evidence of disqualification (e.g., statements showing common ownership 'at the time the invention was made'). Mere fact of same assignee is not, by itself, sufficient. A statement such as 'Application X and Patent Z were, at the time the invention of Application X was made, jointly owned by Companies A and B' would be sufficient. Evidence should identify ownership percentages and the temporal point of ownership. Applicants have an obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to disclose invention dates and lack of common ownership where relevant. In litigation, the patentee similarly bears the burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for claiming 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit in continuing applications
rubrics_metrics.description: An application claiming the benefit of a prior filed copending national or international application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior filed application, and the prior filed application must disclose the named inventor’s invention claimed in at least one claim of the later filed application in the manner provided by the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So long as the applications have at least one inventor in common and the other requirements are met, the Office will permit a claim for 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit without additional submissions regarding inventorship differences. The examiner must examine the earlier filed application to determine common inventorship and that 120 and 37 CFR 1.78 requirements are met; the claim for 120 benefit may be permitted without full examination of the earlier application’s disclosure/support unless intervening references make examination necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and evidentiary elements of a joint research agreement for 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 35 U.S.C. 103(c) purposes, a 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To satisfy 103(c) via a joint research agreement, (1) the claimed invention must be made by or on behalf of parties to the agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (2) the invention must result from activities undertaken within the scope of the agreement; and (3) the patent application must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to the agreement. Example scenarios illustrate when joint-research disqualification prevents a provisional 103 rejection (e.g., two assignees I and J with compliant joint research agreement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice regarding double patenting rejections and terminal disclaimers in commonly owned applications
rubrics_metrics.description: In appropriate circumstances, double patenting rejections may be used in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities; such rejections can be overcome by filing terminal disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director has reinstituted this practice in appropriate circumstances to prevent extensions of patent protection while permitting legitimate benefits. The use of terminal disclaimers and affidavits (e.g., under 37 CFR 1.130, 1.321) are described as means to obviate double patenting rejections when requirements are met. Examiners should consult the Office of Patent Legal Administration (via Technology Center Special Program Examiner) when reissue prosecution may implicate recapture issues for claims amended/cancelled to overcome 103 rejections based on 102(e) art not excluded under 103(c).
